title: Turkey, light or dark meat, fried, coated, skin eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Turkey is a large bird native to North America. The meat can be light (breast) or dark (thighs, drumsticks). When fried in a coating, the skin becomes crispy and edible, while the meat stays juicy. This dish is often served as strips, patties, or breaded pieces seasoned with herbs or spices.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Turkeys were domesticated by Native Americans more than 2,000 years ago.
Light turkey meat contains less fat than dark meat, but both are high‑protein foods.
Fried turkey in a breaded coating is a classic holiday staple in the United States.
When the skin is fried to a golden crust, it adds flavorful fats and aromatic compounds.
Coatings can be made from whole‑grain breadcrumbs, cornflakes, or spice blends, altering texture and taste.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: A 100‑g serving of fried turkey provides about 29 g of high‑quality protein, essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low in saturated fat (light meat)
items.content: Light turkey meat has less saturated fat than many red meats, supporting heart health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Turkey is high in niacin (B3) and vitamin B6, which aid energy metabolism and nervous‑system function.

items.title: Minerals: selenium and zinc
items.content: Selenium acts as an antioxidant, while zinc supports immune function and wound healing.

items.title: Tryptophan
items.content: Tryptophan, present in turkey, is a precursor to serotonin and may help improve mood.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked turkey can harbor Salmonella or Campylobacter; cook to an internal temperature of 74 °C (165 °F).

items.title: High sodium in breading mixes
items.content: Pre‑made coatings often contain salt; choose low‑sodium versions if you monitor blood pressure.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to turkey proteins.

items.title: Calorie density
items.content: Deep‑frying adds calories; portion control is important for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Trans fats from reused oil
items.content: Re‑heating oil repeatedly can create trans fats, which are detrimental to cardiovascular health.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Fried, breaded turkey can be served as a main course, sliced for salads, paired with sauces, placed in sandwiches, or cut into snack‑size bites. The crispy skin is eaten together with the meat. For a lighter option, use olive or sunflower oil and bake instead of deep‑frying.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the cooked turkey to room temperature, then store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑size bags for up to 2 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of 74 °C before serving.
